nameStory: The American Copper gets its name from the brilliant copper-orange color that gleams like a freshly minted penny on its forewings. This metallic sheen catches sunlight beautifully as the butterfly flits through meadows, making it unmistakable among New England's small butterflies.
description: The American Copper is a small, jewel-like butterfly with a wingspan of just 1 to 1.5 inches. Its forewings flash brilliant copper-orange with black spots and borders, while the hindwings are gray-brown with an orange band along the edge. This tiny butterfly is one of our most colorful small species, often seen perching on flowers or basking in sunny spots with wings spread wide.

idTips.label: Copper forewings
idTips.description: The forewings shine like polished copper pennies with bold black spots scattered across the orange surface and thick black borders - no other small butterfly has this metallic orange gleam

idTips.label: Gray hindwings with orange edge
idTips.description: The back wings are muted gray-brown with a distinctive bright orange stripe running along the outer edge, creating a beautiful contrast with the fiery forewings

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: About the size of a quarter when wings are spread, making it one of our smallest butterflies - you might mistake it for a moth at first glance

idTips.label: Black spots and markings
idTips.description: Look for neat black dots scattered across the copper forewings and small black markings on the hindwings that look almost like tiny eyes

idTips.label: Rapid, erratic flight
idTips.description: Flies in quick, darting movements close to the ground, often landing frequently to bask in sunny spots with wings held horizontally

idTips.label: Threadlike antennae
idTips.description: Has thin, delicate antennae with small clubs at the tips, typical of the gossamer-wing family - much thinner than those of skippers

habitat: Look for American Coppers in open, sunny areas like old fields, meadows, roadsides, and disturbed ground throughout New England. They particularly love areas where their host plant, sheep sorrel, grows abundantly - often in acidic soils and waste places. You'll find them from sea level to moderate elevations, especially in areas with a mix of flowers for nectar and weedy plants.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late April and May, with fresh, bright copper wings that really catch the eye. Look for mating pairs and females laying tiny white eggs on sheep sorrel leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time with multiple generations - you'll see the most individuals from June through August. Adults are most active during warm, sunny afternoons when they're easiest to spot nectaring on flowers.
seasonality.fall: A final generation emerges in September and early October, though these individuals may be slightly smaller and less vibrant than spring butterflies. Last adults disappear with the first hard frosts.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as caterpillars on host plants, hidden and dormant until spring warmth triggers their development into pupae.

funFact: American Copper caterpillars are actually tended by ants like tiny livestock - the caterpillars produce a sweet honeydew that the ants harvest, and in return, the ants protect the caterpillars from predators and parasites!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with small skippers, but skippers have thicker bodies, hooked antennae, and usually hold their wings at angles rather than spread flat. Remember: if it gleams like copper and sits with wings spread wide like it's sunbathing, it's your American Copper.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, the American Copper is actually found across much of the northern hemisphere - it's the same species as the Small Copper in Europe. In some field guides, you might see it listed under its scientific name or called simply 'Copper,' which can be confusing since there are other copper butterflies in western North America.
compareHints: The American Copper is the only member of its genus regularly found in New England, making it relatively easy to identify. Compared to other gossamer-wings like blues and hairstreaks, it's distinguished by that unmistakable copper-orange color - blues are predominantly blue (obviously!) and hairstreaks typically have thin 'tails' on their hindwings plus more subdued colors.
